title: Limit laws and the squeeze theorem
section: Limits of Sequences ▷ Algebra and estimates
terms: sum law; product law; quotient law; squeeze theorem; sandwich theorem; bounded factor times null sequence; growth comparison.

exposition.text:
For convergent real sequences, limits commute with sums and products, and with quotients
when the denominator limit is nonzero. If u ≤ a ≤ v eventually and both outer sequences
n n n
tend to L, then a → L. In particular, a bounded sequence times a sequence tending to zero
n
−p n
tends to zero. Powers n tend to zero for p > 0, and r → 0 when |r| < 1.
Divide rational expressions by the dominant power and rationalize differences of nearly equal
radicals. Do not use quotient laws with a zero denominator limit, or subtract two divergent
infinities as if they were numbers. A function limit f(x) → L as x → ∞ implies f (n) → L, but
the converse is false: integer samples do not control intervening values.

question.text:
A continuous function f : R → R satisfies f (n) = 0 for every positive integer n. Which
conclusion follows?
(A) f(x) → 0 as x → ∞.
(B) f is bounded.
(C) f(x)/x → 0 as x → ∞.
(D) lim f(n) = 0, but none of the preceding three conclusions is forced.
n→∞
(E) f must be identically zero.

solution.text:
2
The sampled sequence is identically zero. However, f(x) = x sin(πx) is continuous and
vanishes at every integer while being unbounded, lacking a limit at infinity, and having
f(x)/x = x sin(πx) fail to tend to zero. Discrete samples do not control intervening values.
